sections.h2: Does Ohio charge an estate tax?
sections.html:
No. House Bill 153 repealed the Ohio estate tax for every estate with a date of death in 2013 or later. House Bill 110 of the 134th General Assembly then closed the books on older estates: nothing is owed on property first discovered after December 31, 2021, or on property found earlier but never disclosed or reported by that date.

A family selling an inherited Ohio house therefore files no state estate tax return before closing. The state has also dropped the requirement for ET 12, 13 and 14 release forms before a decedent's assets move to another person, and county auditors and banks have been asked to stop forwarding them.

Only a very large estate owes it. The basic exclusion amount for a 2026 death is $15,000,000, a figure raised by Public Law 119-21, which was signed July 4, 2025. One house rarely comes close, so for most families the federal return does not set the timeline.

Two further points apply. An estate that does not have to file a federal return should skip Form 8971. When a spouse survives, the estate may elect on a timely return to hand the unused exclusion to that spouse.

sections.h2: Who signs the deed on an inherited Ohio house
sections.html:
Usually the executor or administrator, working under the probate court of the decedent's home county. Ohio's land-sale procedure for executors, administrators and guardians runs from R.C. 2127.01 through 2127.43. An executor whose will grants a power of sale may follow the will instead.

Smaller estates may skip full administration. R.C. 2113.03 lets the court release an estate from administration at $35,000 in assets or under. The ceiling is $100,000 if a surviving spouse takes everything. The order can direct delivery of personal property and transfer of real property, and the court may name a commissioner to sign the conveyance papers. A buyer who pays value in good faith gets the same protection from unsecured creditors that administration would give.

  • Ask the probate clerk whether the estate fits a release or needs letters of authority.
  • Gather the death certificate, the will, and the vesting deed.
  • Order a title search early so liens surface before a buyer finds them.

Title may already belong to a named beneficiary. Under R.C. 5302.22, an owner may record a verified transfer on death designation affidavit with the county recorder while still alive. When the owner dies, title vests in the beneficiaries the affidavit names.

Nobody has to pay for it or receive it for it to work. The recorder charges the deed fee and files it under the owner's name. Heirs who think a parent signed one should ask the recorder to search that name. Knowingly false statements in the affidavit count as falsification under R.C. 2921.13.

sections.h2: Taxes when an heir sells the house
sections.html:
An heir's taxable gain starts from basis. For inherited property that is generally the fair market value on the date of death. Estates that elected the alternate valuation date use that figure instead, and farm or business land can use special-use valuation. An heir who never received a Schedule A (Form 8971) from the executor can rely on the appraised date-of-death value used for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes.

Order an appraisal early and keep it with the estate papers so the tax preparer can apply it to the final price.

Who handles each step of an inherited-house sale in Ohio
StepOffice and statute
Release from administration or land saleProbate court, R.C. 2113.03 and R.C. 2127.01
Transfer on death affidavit searchCounty recorder, R.C. 5302.22
County transfer tax paid at deed deliveryCounty auditor, R.C. 322.02
Valuation complaintCounty auditor, then board of revision, R.C. 5715.19

R.C. 322.02 caps any county transfer levy at thirty cents for each hundred dollars of value. The grantor pays it at the auditor's office before the deed is recorded. Ask the county auditor which rate your house falls under.

An owner can. R.C. 5715.19 routes a valuation complaint through the county auditor. The filing date is March 31 of the following tax year, unless first-half collection closes later. The county board of revision decides it. A second complaint on the same parcel in the same interim period is barred unless conditions changed. Examples are an arm's length sale, a casualty loss or a substantial improvement.

A date-of-death appraisal can support a complaint when the county figure looks high. The auditor's office can tell you which tax year a new filing would cover.

sections.h2: What buyers and title companies ask the estate for
sections.html:
The first thing a title company wants is proof of who can sign. It will not insure a deed whose chain it cannot follow. For an estate in administration, that is the executor's or administrator's letters of authority from the probate court. For a released estate, it is a copy of the release order. If a transfer on death affidavit covers the house, bring the recorded affidavit and a death certificate.

The title company will also search for mortgages, judgments and unpaid tax. Ohio land sales by fiduciaries follow the statute, so a sale that skips the court steps can leave a buyer with a cloud on title. If the file is tangled, a probate attorney in the home county can confirm which documents the closing will need before you accept an offer.

sections.h2: Where an Ohio heir should start
sections.html:
Begin with whatever decides who may sign, then turn to the house. The probate clerk is the first call.

  • Find the original will and file it with the probate court if no one has.
  • Keep the house insured and secured, and redirect the mail.
  • Ask the recorder whether a transfer on death affidavit exists.
  • Request the current tax bill from the county treasurer.
  • Order the date-of-death appraisal.

Timeline for planning: the probate clerk's answer on authority comes first, since nothing can be listed with confidence until you know who signs. A title search and the payoff of any mortgage follow. Valuation questions and the county transfer tax can be sorted out in parallel. A buyer who pays cash does not need a lender to approve the estate's paperwork, but the title company still does, so gather the letters or release order before you list.

When the family wants out fast, a cash buyer who accepts the house in its current condition can remove the repair list and the open houses. If that fits, compare offers by what the estate keeps after transfer tax, payoffs and costs. Those items apply whichever way the house sells, so the real difference is time and certainty.

faqs.q: Does Ohio have an estate tax in 2026?
faqs.a: No. The tax was repealed for estates with a 2013 or later date of death, and the House Bill 110 sunset ended collection on property first discovered after December 31, 2021.

faqs.q: Do I need a state tax release to transfer a parent's Ohio house?
faqs.a: No. The ET 12, 13 and 14 release forms are no longer required. Title and probate steps still apply, so ask the probate court clerk what the estate needs.

faqs.q: Is there a federal estate tax on a modest Ohio estate?
faqs.a: Not at that size. For 2026 deaths the federal basic exclusion amount is $15,000,000. Below that, an estate does not need to file Form 706 on account of size.

faqs.q: Can a house pass without full probate in Ohio?
faqs.a: Sometimes. A recorded transfer on death affidavit vests title in the named beneficiary under R.C. 5302.22, and a probate court can release an estate with $35,000 or less in assets under R.C. 2113.03. The probate court can tell you which path fits.

faqs.q: Who owes the county transfer tax on an estate sale in Ohio?
faqs.a: The seller named in the deed. R.C. 322.02 puts the charge on the grantor, payable to the county auditor before the deed reaches the recorder, at a rate each county sets within the thirty-cent cap.
